extracted.intended_audience: aspiring screenwriters, filmmakers, producers, and general readers interested in film/TV/theatre industry practices
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive norms about the role of a script doctor — a writer hired to rewrite or improve an existing film, television, or theatre script — including what they are asked to fix, when they are brought in, credit rules, and common practices/risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspects of a script to improve
rubrics_metrics.description: Script doctors are hired to rewrite an existing script or improve specific aspects of it, including structure, characterization, dialogue, pacing, themes, and other elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enumerates the common dimensions script doctors are expected to address; work can range from small 'punch-ups' (e.g., jokes, snappy lines) to broader structural fixes. Examples in the article illustrate interventions on dialogue, third-act problems, and general 'sprucing up.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical timing of intervention (development/pre-production)
rubrics_metrics.description: They are usually brought in for scripts that have been almost 'green-lit' during the development and pre-production phases of a film to address specific issues with the script, as identified by the financiers, production team, and cast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Script doctors often work late in development — sometimes in the 'ninth inning' — focusing on fixes needed immediately before shooting; this constrains the scope of acceptable changes and favors targeted, fast solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writers Guild of America credit thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: To receive credit under the Writers Guild of America screenwriting credit system requires a second screenwriter to contribute more than 50 percent of an original screenplay or 33 percent of an adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because script doctors typically do not meet these thresholds, they generally do their work uncredited. This rule explains industry credit practices and why many high-profile doctors remain invisible on screen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mandates and tasks ('production polish', 'punch up')
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical mandates include 'production polish' (late-stage fixes), inserting jokes or 'punching up' dialogue, fixing the big climax/third act, making sequences cheaper, and resuscitating a film after poor test screenings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by practitioners: Sorkin describes being asked for 'snappy dialogue' and 'production polish'; Whedon and de Souza recount mandates to 'punch up the big climax, the third act' or to rewrite and re-cut following bad tests. These are concrete, recurring task-types for script doctors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limits: polish vs story-breaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Script doctors are often expected not to 'break the story' but to provide polish — e.g., improve dialogue and finish touches rather than reimagine core plot or moving parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sorkin contrasts 'production polish' with deeper story work: when brought in late, the job may be expressly to add lines or tweak scenes rather than restructure the narrative. This informs what kinds of interventions are acceptable in late-stage rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criterion for accepting jobs
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual script doctors may accept work based on whether there is a 'germ of an idea' they would actually like to see or whether they can help others tell their stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: John Sayles' stated approach: he takes jobs when the material contains something he finds worth pursuing. This is a subjective professional standard guiding which projects a script doctor will invest time in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial and artistic reasons for working uncredited
rubrics_metrics.description: Script doctors generally do their work uncredited for a variety of commercial and artistic reasons, including guild credit rules, not wanting association with projects that fail, or other professional choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being uncredited can be deliberate (avoid association) or compulsory (WGA thresholds); the article gives multiple practitioner perspectives on why high-profile writers accept uncredited work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical risks and anti-patterns for script doctors
rubrics_metrics.description: Studios may require submission of notes as unpaid work and then use ideas without hiring the writer; writers risk being arbitrated out of credit, having drafts thrown out, or being invited to read-throughs after their draft was discarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carrie Fisher describes 'life-wasting events' where notes are taken but the writer isn't hired; Whedon recounts being arbitrated out of credit and having drafts discarded. These are warnings about exploitative or demoralising industry practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility and acknowledgement outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcomes vary: some script doctors remain completely uncredited, some are credited as 'creative consultant', and in some cases themes or fixes survive while no words of the doctor appear in the final film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tom Stoppard claims 'I don't think there's a single word of mine in the film' despite thematic influence; others have been credited in varying ways. Expect low public visibility for much of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Script doctors are frequently highly paid for brief periods, described as 'handsome fees' or 'overpaid' by practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not a formal rule, the article repeatedly notes that late-stage script doctors can command substantial pay for short engagements — a practical consideration for both writers and production companies hiring them.
